stops.name: San Nicolás de los Arroyos: la derrota final del año Veinte
stops.campa: His force entrenches at San Nicolás and there, on 2 August, the troops of Buenos Aires crush it: the last army Carlos de Alvear will ever lead against his own city. The adventure of the year Twenty is over; Carrera rides north toward his death, and Alvear goes back down the river to Montevideo with nothing. The canon closes the darkest chapter here and marks the turn of the arc: from this lowest water, every step of the rest of his life ascends.

stops.name: Montevideo: el segundo destierro
stops.campa: Again Montevideo, again the exile's lodging in the conquered city of his youth: poorer now, twice proscribed, his name a curse in the mouths of unitarios and federales alike. He waits out the turn of the wheel as the province he cannot enter reorganizes itself under Martín Rodríguez and a minister named Rivadavia, who is building a state that will need generals and ambassadors. The canon lets the exile season: the bowstring is at full draw.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: la rehabilitación
stops.campa: The law of oblivion opens the gates: in 1822 Alvear returns to Buenos Aires, his rank of brigadier general restored, his sequestered goods unwound, his sword reclaimed for the state by the ministry of Rivadavia. Seven years after the water-gate of the proscribed, the fallen angel walks the Plaza again and the city that burned his name finds it needs precisely his gifts: languages, courts, lodges, war. The canon calls this the second founding of Alvear: what was buried in 1815 rises in 1822 as the Republic's first diplomat.

stops.name: Londres: la misión ante Canning
stops.campa: The government sends its rehabilitated general across the ocean he knows too well: Alvear in London again, thirteen years after the lodge of Grafton Way, now as envoy of a state seeking its place among nations. He treats with George Canning's Foreign Office in the very season the minister resolves to recognize the new republics of America: Buenos Aires among the first. The city of the oath has become the city of the recognition, and the canon lingers on the symmetry: the conspirator of 1811 returns as the credentialed proof that the conspiracy succeeded.

stops.name: Washington: recibido por el presidente Monroe
stops.campa: In mid-October 1824 President James Monroe receives the general in Washington, and John Quincy Adams, Secretary of State, opens to him the reasoning of the Doctrine that bears the President's name: the Americas closed to new European conquest. Alvear is the first great figure of the Argentine revolution to stand in the President's house: soldier of Tudela, founder of lodges, ex-Director, now reading the new hemisphere at its northern pole. The canon notes that the North receives him twice: now in honor, and at the end, forever.

stops.name: Nueva York: la primera vista del puerto
stops.campa: Before turning home the envoy passes through New York and sees for the first time the forest of masts, the packet ships, the brick city climbing its island: the great commercial republic working like an engine. He studies it as he studied every battlefield, and the tradition sets down the omen without comment, as omens are set down: of all the harbors of his wandering life, this northern one, the farthest from the Misiones, is the harbor where the arc will close.

stops.name: Potosí: la misión ante Bolívar
stops.campa: Named minister to the Libertador, Alvear climbs the Andes with José Miguel Díaz Vélez and in October 1825 stands before Simón Bolívar in Potosí. The commission is double: to consent, in the name of the Provinces, that Upper Peru decide its own destiny (Bolivia is being born that very season) and to draw the Liberator's sword into the coming war against the Empire of Brazil for the Banda Oriental. Bolívar dazzles, promises, and does not march. The two summits of the continental revolution measure each other in the thin air, and part with embraces and without an army.

stops.name: Cerro Rico de Potosí: las banderas en la cumbre
stops.campa: On 26 October the Liberator ascends the Cerro Rico with Sucre and his staff, and with the Argentine envoys Alvear and Díaz Vélez at his side, and on the summit of the silver mountain that fed three centuries of empire the flags of the new republics are unfurled. Bolívar speaks of the journey from the Orinoco to this peak as the completion of the war of the continent. Alvear of the Misiones stands witness on the roof of the revolution: the man of the Atlantic wound present at the Andean consummation. The canon keeps the scene as one of its high altars.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: ministro de Guerra y Marina
stops.campa: The war with the Empire of Brazil is already burning on the sea and the frontier when President Rivadavia calls Alvear to the Ministry of War and Marine. The ex-Director organizes what he once embodied: remounts, arsenals, recruitment, Brown's squadron, the Army of Observation on the Uruguay. The state that broke him in 1815 now hands him its whole military machine, for the canon's plain reason: no other living man has taken a fortified city, presided a sovereign assembly and studied war under Napoleon's marshals. The instrument and the hour have found each other.

stops.name: Campamento del Arroyo Grande, Entre Ríos: el mando del Ejército Republicano
stops.campa: In the first days of 1827 Alvear takes command in person of the Army of the Republic in its camps on the Uruguay, seven to eight thousand veterans, gauchos and orientales, with Lavalle, Paz, Mansilla, Iriarte, Lavalleja, Soler under his hand: every sword of the age in one order of battle. He drills them hard, reorganizes the cavalry, and then does the unexpected thing the canon loves: he does not wait to defend Entre Ríos, but crosses the frontier and invades the Rio Grande, carrying the war back into the very Misiones country where he was born.

stops.name: Arroyo Bacacay, Rio Grande do Sul: el sable de Lavalle
stops.campa: The campaign of maneuvers begins to bite. At the Bacacay stream, on 13 February, Lavalle's cavalry, the striking edge of Alvear's plan, falls on the advance of Bento Manuel Ribeiro and cuts it up. The imperial columns, drawn deep into their own province by Alvear's feints and countermarches, begin to bleed at every contact. The canon reads the week as a single composition: Bacacay is the first phrase of the masterpiece, written with Lavalle's sabres to Alvear's score.

stops.name: Rincón del Ombú: Mansilla dispersa a Bento Manuel
stops.campa: Three days after Bacacay, at the Ombú, General Mansilla with infantry and horse scatters Bento Manuel's cavalry again. The imperial army under the Marquis of Barbacena, harassed, misled and hungry, hurries to catch the Republicans before they cross the Santa María, exactly as Alvear intends. The canon underlines the craft: the victor of these plains is not improvising valor but conducting an army like an orchestra, drawing the enemy hour by hour onto the ground he has already chosen for the twentieth of February.
